_comment: Sources whose CLAIMS the project rests on, to be harvested as raw text.
Why this file exists. Research reached this project through WebFetch, which
returns a small model's summary of a page rather than the page. Every claim
sourced that way is second-hand, and several are load-bearing: the Princeton
GEO percentages, MonetaryGrant being the underused schema type, what the
competitors actually do. The sandbox's egress proxy denies all of these hosts
to both curl and WebFetch, and the allowlist narrowed mid-session, so four
domains that answered earlier now return 403.
The crawler already solves this for scholarship pages: it runs on a GitHub
runner with open egress, flattens HTML to text, and COMMITS the text. That is
the property WebFetch lacks. Harvested text is permanent, greppable, and
re-readable by any future session, so a claim can be checked against the
source months later rather than trusted because I said so.
follow is 0 deliberately. These are specific documents, not hubs to explore,
and link-following on a blog would pull in its whole archive.

seeds.note: THE primary source. Every percentage we cite (+115% citations, +30-40% statistics and quotations, 22-41% overall) came from secondary reporting. Verify the real figures and which of the nine methods were tested.
Confirm the properties we emit are real: amount, funder, sameAs, areaServed. Invalid properties are silently dropped, so a mistake here is invisible.
The type we replaced. Check whether applicationDeadline and applicationStartDate would let us carry deadlines in schema, which MonetaryGrant appears not to support.

Google restricted FAQ rich results in 2023 to authoritative government and health sites. If FAQPage no longer earns anything in Google, its value here is answer engines only, which changes how much weight it deserves.
The largest technical risk to a templated site. Our 3-award and 6-field indexability bars were set from secondary summaries, not this text.
